title: Training-Inference Kernel Contracts:Bounding Divergence in Post-Training and Deployment

paper.title: Training-Inference Kernel Contracts: Bounding Divergence in Post-Training and Deployment
paper.abstract: Abstract A modern post-training pipeline writes one symbol for its policy, π θ \pi_{\theta} , and evaluates it through two different programs: a training kernel running autograd with high-precision accumulators against fixed shapes, and an inference kernel that fuses low-precision operators behind a paged key–value cache and adapts attention tiles to the workload. In finite precision the two programs compute measurably different functions of the same weights, with the gap concentrated on slices that aggregate benchmarks under-represent. Off-policy bias in reinforcement-learning rollouts, slice-level regressions under FP8 deployment, calibration drift between fine-tuning and serving, and benchmark scores that fail to reproduce across hardware fleets are facets of this same gap. We formalize the gap as a missing index on π θ \pi_{\theta} and propose a small specification that names it: a kernel contract 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) of numerical, statistical, runtime, and observability clauses with an escalation policy from violations to routing actions. We derive a chain of Lipschitz-style bounds connecting the four families: a single numerical clause on logit drift propagates through total-variation distance into a bound on any bounded reward, with explicit constants. Specialising the chain to RL post-training, we show that a per-token bound on the importance ratio w = π θ K train ​ ( y ∣ x ) / π θ K inf ​ ( y ∣ x ) w=\pi^{K_{\mathrm{train}}}_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\pi^{K_{\mathrm{inf}}}_{\theta}(y\mid x) bounds the bias of the standard policy-gradient estimator under explicit support and norm assumptions, and reinterprets PPO-style ratio clipping as a budget on the train–infer kernel pair rather than only on the policy update. A four-stage promotion pipeline (offline CI, shadow, canary, full) and an online routing loop enforce the contract once a model is deployed. A minimal YAML DSL with a sketched reference implementation ( Appendices A and C ) shows what a deployable artifact of this form looks like. This is a framework and vocabulary paper: we do not report empirical validation at production scale, and we do not claim that kernel divergence is the sole cause of the failure modes the framework addresses.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: In a modern post-training pipeline, the symbol π θ \pi_{\theta} denotes two different functions in finite precision. The training path evaluates π θ \pi_{\theta} through a program built around autograd: high-precision accumulators, fixed-shape batches, reference attention, and an operator graph optimised for differentiability. The serving path evaluates it through fused low-precision kernels [ 15 , 5 , 14 ] , a paged key–value cache [ 13 ] , and attention tiles whose sizes depend on the workload [ 2 , 3 , 22 ] . The two programs share parameter tensors and almost nothing else, and the resulting numerical difference is not uniform across inputs: aggregate benchmarks can move within noise while a long-context slice or a safety-critical prompt class moves an order of magnitude more. Reinforcement-learning post-training exposes the same gap. Pipelines such as PPO [ 21 , 17 ] and GRPO [ 23 ] generate rollouts on an inference engine and apply gradients computed on a training engine; the standard estimator’s derivation treats the two as the same policy. The implied per-token importance ratio between rollout time and gradient time is assumed equal to one and is absorbed without flag when it is not, which biases the gradient in a way that does not appear in the training loss and surfaces only later as KL collapse, reward hacking, or sudden reward degradation. The documented fragility of large-scale RLHF to implementation detail [ 8 , 4 , 1 , 11 ] is consistent with this mechanism. The same conflation surfaces wherever the training and inference paths run different programs against the same weights: calibration schedules tuned with K train K_{\mathrm{train}} misfire on probabilities produced by K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} ; benchmark scores diverge across hardware fleets whose unit tests all pass; red-team prompts that fail on one stack pass on the other. We treat them as facets of one specification gap: no pipeline says, in machine-readable form, what divergence between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} it is willing to tolerate, on which slices. This paper develops the object that specifies the gap. A kernel contract is a tuple 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) of numerical, statistical, runtime, and observability clauses with an escalation policy that maps violations to routing actions. The contract sits next to the model checkpoint and the kernel build, is versioned with them, and travels with the artifact through CI and into deployment. Bit-level equivalence is not the target; the inference kernel exists to trade low-level equivalence for throughput, and the trade is worth making. The target is to specify which equivalences are required, where, and what to do when they fail. Section 2 fixes notation and makes the kernel index on π θ \pi_{\theta} explicit. Section 3 collects four failure modes whose shared structure motivates the framework. Section 4 introduces the contract formally. Section 5 derives the Lipschitz-style chain that turns a clause on logit drift into a clause on reward drift. Section 6 specialises the chain to RL post-training. Section 7 describes the four-stage promotion pipeline; Section 8 lays out an experimental protocol against which the framework’s predictions can be tested. Three contributions follow. (i) Conceptual : the right specifiable object in a modern LLM pipeline is the pair ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) together with the slice scope on which they are required to agree, not the checkpoint or the engine alone. (ii) Technical : the chain of Section 5 lets contract authors specify at the level they can measure and inherit guarantees at the level they care about. (iii) Applied : under explicit support and norm assumptions ( Section 6 ), a per-token bound on the importance ratio bounds the policy-gradient bias of the standard estimator, and the PPO clipping range ϵ \epsilon acquires a second interpretation as a budget on the train–infer kernel pair.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: This paper proposes a framework and vocabulary. It does not claim that kernel divergence is the sole cause of the failure modes it discusses, does not report empirical validation at production scale, and does not provide a deployable open-source implementation. Section 8 lays out the protocol against which the framework’s predictions can be tested; Appendices A and C specify, in sketch form, what an implementation that consumes its declarative artifacts would look like.

sections.heading: 2.2 Contracted convergence and violation levels
sections.text: A contract 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is a structured collection of clauses, each constraining one of these drift quantities on a designated slice. Convergence is defined relative to 𝒞 \mathcal{C} rather than to any single scalar. Definition 1 (Contracted convergence) . Let 𝒞 \mathcal{C} have hard-clause set ℋ \mathcal{H} and soft-clause set 𝒮 \mathcal{S} with exceedance budgets { ρ i } i ∈ 𝒮 \{\rho_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{S}} . The pair ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) is 𝒞 \mathcal{C} -convergent on D eval D_{\mathrm{eval}} if every h ∈ ℋ h\in\mathcal{H} holds on every slice it applies to, and every s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} satisfies Pr x ∼ D eval [ m s ( x ) > τ s ] ≤ ρ s \Pr_{x\sim D_{\mathrm{eval}}}[m_{s}(x)>\tau_{s}]\leq\rho_{s} . The definition gives a contract-relative, slice-aware, behaviour-tied answer to the implicit question of when an inference build is equivalent to a training build for the purpose of shipping a model. Each violation is then assigned one of three severity levels: L1 (informational) is logged; L2 (quality-impacting) triggers a guarded route or promotion freeze; L3 (safety- or correctness-critical) triggers immediate fallback to a known-good kernel. The three-level vocabulary is the minimum required to turn telemetry into action; Sections 4 and 7 embed it inside the full specification and serving pipeline.

sections.heading: 3.2 FP8 deployment of a BF16-trained model
sections.text: Casting a BF16-trained model to FP8 at deployment is routine [ 15 ] . The choice of FP8 format (E4M3 vs E5M2), per-tensor vs per-channel scaling, and cast placement inside fused operators each shift the output distribution. A model within noise of its BF16 reference on aggregate benchmarks can still drift on rare safety prompts (refusal flips), on structured outputs (JSON parseability, tool-call schemas), and on long-context tasks where per-step errors accumulate. The cast does not change θ \theta but it changes the kernel that evaluates θ \theta , and the deployed function differs from the one the eval was run on. Slice-aware clauses in 𝒩 \mathcal{N} and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} make the difference visible.

sections.heading: 3.3 Attention kernel substitution
sections.text: The FlashAttention family [ 2 , 3 , 22 ] is mathematically equivalent to standard scaled dot-product attention in exact arithmetic, but variants differ in summation order, tile sizes, and accumulator precision. In finite precision the resulting logits disagree by amounts small in ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm but capable of flipping the top-1 token at low-margin steps. In autoregressive generation a single flipped token alters the conditioning for every subsequent step, so a small numerical disagreement compounds into a large behavioural one. The framework treats this as a numerical clause whose threshold is set by the margin distribution on the relevant slices.

sections.heading: 3.4 Heterogeneous serving fleets
sections.text: A deployed model is served by a fleet of heterogeneous accelerators (H100, MI300X, B200) with slightly different kernel builds. Two replicas can return different outputs for the same request, and the replica is chosen by routing and capacity rather than request content. Without a contract over cross-kernel agreement, A/B tests, evaluations, and safety audits become non-reproducible in ways difficult to attribute. The fleet is effectively serving from a family { π θ K 1 , … , π θ K m } \{\pi^{K_{1}}_{\theta},\dots,\pi^{K_{m}}_{\theta}\} while reporting metrics as if from a single π θ \pi_{\theta} . A contract makes the equivalence class of acceptable kernels explicit so that routing is a certified action.

sections.heading: Common pattern.
sections.text: In each case a single notational object π θ \pi_{\theta} papers over a kernel-indexed family { π θ K } K \{\pi^{K}_{\theta}\}_{K} whose members, in finite precision, compute different functions of the same weights. The phenomenon each case names is the family viewed from a different angle; the rest of the paper develops one specification that addresses all four.

sections.heading: 4 The kernel contract
sections.text: The cases of Section 3 share a missing piece: an explicit specification of acceptable train–infer divergence and the operational response to its violation. A kernel contract is a tuple 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) , \mathcal{C}\;=\;(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi), (8) with 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 \mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O} clause sets covering numerical, statistical, runtime, and observability properties of ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) and Π \Pi the escalation policy mapping violations to routing actions. Each clause is a record γ = ( id , m , τ , Σ , ρ , λ , π ) , \gamma\;=\;\bigl(\,\mathrm{id},\;m,\;\tau,\;\Sigma,\;\rho,\;\lambda,\;\pi\,\bigr), (9) with id \mathrm{id} a stable identifier, m m a drift metric from Section 2 , τ \tau its threshold, Σ ⊆ { S i } \Sigma\subseteq\{S_{i}\} the slices it applies to, ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \rho\in[0,1] the allowed exceedance rate ( ρ = 0 \rho=0 marks the clause hard), λ ∈ { L1 , L2 , L3 } \lambda\in\{\mathrm{L1,L2,L3}\} its violation level, and π \pi the remediation drawn from Π \Pi . Every clause must be reproducible from logged inputs and traces alone: a clause that cannot be re-evaluated post hoc on the same request cannot underwrite a deployment decision.

sections.heading: 4.1 The four families
sections.text: The four-family split corresponds to the four axes along which one program can differ from another while both execute the same weights: type level (what each program computes), behavioural level (how the induced distributions act under realistic decoding), environmental level (how the program behaves under real batch shapes, concurrency, and capacity), and epistemic level (what the program must reveal about itself so the other three remain checkable). Drop any one and the framework loses an axis large-scale deployments are already paying for. Numerical ( 𝒩 \mathcal{N} ) owns percentile bounds on Δ logit \Delta_{\mathrm{logit}} , Δ KL \Delta_{\mathrm{KL}} , Δ TV \Delta_{\mathrm{TV}} ; bounds on 𝔼 ⁡ [ w ​ log ⁡ w ] \mathbb{E}[w\log w] for the RL importance ratio of Section 3.1 ; and deterministic-replay equivalence on a controlled input subset. It catches failure modes originating in low-level numerics (FP8 casts, attention-tile changes, kernel substitution). Statistical ( 𝒮 \mathcal{S} ) owns top- k k agreement on critical slices, calibration drift Δ ECE \Delta_{\mathrm{ECE}} , reward and refusal-rate deltas within Δ r \Delta_{r} , and structured-output parseability gaps—failure modes invisible at the logit level but visible after sampling. Runtime ( ℛ \mathcal{R} ) owns latency percentiles, throughput floors, memory ceilings (including the KV cache), failure-rate ceilings, and a determinism window—identical inputs in the same shard must produce identical outputs within tolerance δ \delta . Observability ( 𝒪 \mathcal{O} ) owns required trace fields, replay signatures, kernel fingerprints, and event schemas; a contract without it is unenforceable, since unattributable violations are operationally indistinguishable from no violation.

sections.heading: 4.3 Contracts as versioned artifacts
sections.text: A contract is itself a versioned artifact that travels with both checkpoints and kernel builds. The artifact register stores ( θ ​ -hash , K inf ​ -hash , 𝒞 ​ -hash ) (\theta\text{-hash},K_{\mathrm{inf}}\text{-hash},\mathcal{C}\text{-hash}) triples, and every promotion records the triple it was evaluated against. This makes deployment decisions auditable and lets post-incident analysis distinguish a contract that was too loose from a kernel build that regressed from a model update that interacted badly with an existing contract—three failure modes with three different fixes.

sections.heading: 6 Application: RL post-training
sections.text: The chain of Section 5 specialises sharply to reinforcement-learning post-training, where the conflation of π θ K train \pi^{K_{\mathrm{train}}}_{\theta} and π θ K inf \pi^{K_{\mathrm{inf}}}_{\theta} becomes an estimator bias rather than a quality drift. The same kernel mismatch that costs a few benchmark points in supervised deployment biases the policy-gradient signal that is supposed to steer the model away from those losses. This section makes the bias explicit, bounds it under stated assumptions, and reads the standard literature through the resulting lens.

sections.heading: 6.1 Assumptions and scope
sections.text: Throughout this section we work at the per-token level. Let x x be a prompt-and-history context and y ∈ 𝒱 y\in\mathcal{V} the next token. sections.heading: 6.5 Reading the RL literature through this lens
sections.text: Two persistent observations in the RL literature become legible through the contract framing. The first is the documented fragility of large-scale RLHF to implementation detail [ 8 , 4 , 1 ] : reward hacking, KL collapse, sudden drops in eval scores. Much of this catalogue is consistent with silent violation of N-RLHF-2 as the policy drifts away from the inference engine’s calibrated regime, and the standard remedies (smaller batches, lower learning rates, more frequent reference resets) all reduce the magnitude of 𝔼 ⁡ [ w ​ log ⁡ w ] \mathbb{E}[w\log w] without naming what they are doing. The second is that organisations who pin their RL stack to a single kernel build often report stable training: they are operating inside an implicit contract they happen to satisfy. Writing the contract down is what separates a working recipe from a transferable engineering practice, and it is what makes the next kernel migration auditable rather than terrifying. With the contract defined, its guarantees established, and its scope made explicit, the remaining question is operational. Section 7 describes how a pipeline evaluates and enforces a contract once a model is deployed.

sections.heading: 7 Enforcement
sections.text: A contract that nothing checks is a document, not an interface. The four families have different evaluation needs: 𝒩 \mathcal{N} checks offline because it does not depend on traffic; 𝒮 \mathcal{S} needs representative traffic because behaviour depends on what is sampled; ℛ \mathcal{R} requires live serving conditions because micro-benchmarks do not predict tail behaviour under contention; 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is the precondition that makes the other three checkable. A four-stage promotion pipeline allocates each family to its venue, and an online routing loop converts continuous measurements into actions.

sections.heading: 7.1 Four-stage promotion
sections.text: Every change under review—weight update, kernel build, routing change, hardware rebalance—traverses the same four stages. Offline CI: all hard 𝒩 \mathcal{N} clauses and a deterministic subset of 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , ℛ \mathcal{R} , 𝒪 \mathcal{O} are evaluated against a fixed evaluation set with pinned slice definitions; any hard violation blocks promotion and returns the candidate with a named clause and per-slice breakdown. Shadow: a fraction of live traffic is mirrored through the candidate K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} without exposing its responses to users, catching workload-dependent regressions the fixed eval set under-represents. Canary: a small live traffic fraction α ∈ ( 0 , α max ] \alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\max}] is routed to the candidate with Π \Pi active; L2 triggers guarded routing, L3 triggers rollback. Full promotion occurs only after sustained compliance over a stability window of duration W W at the canary fraction, catching slow-onset regressions (for example, KV-cache fragmentation that takes hours to surface). The four stages catch four different failure classes; skipping any leaves that class unmonitored.

sections.heading: 7.3 Observability and continuous re-evaluation
sections.text: Observability is what makes the rest auditable. Kernels emit build fingerprints (compiler version, FA variant, quantisation configuration, hardware target), per-request shape, RNG seed, sampling parameters, and replay signatures hashing intermediate tensors at audit points. Given those artifacts, any flagged request can be replayed under both K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} and the per-source decomposition of Section 5 attributed to a specific subsystem. Pre-deployment validation is necessary but not sufficient: hardware drivers, kernel libraries, and traffic distributions all evolve, so a subset of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is re-evaluated continuously in shadow against live traffic, and any change to 𝒞 \mathcal{C} itself traverses the same four-stage path as a code change.

sections.heading: 8 Experimental protocol
sections.text: A framework that cannot be tested is a framework that cannot be wrong. The five families below each make a falsifiable prediction. E1 tests the assumptions of Section 5 ; E2 stresses them across hardware and shape; E3 tests the central RL bound of Proposition 2 and its corrective clause; E4 and E5 test two of the directions of Section 9 .

sections.heading: 8.1 E1. Numerical drift baseline
sections.text: Goal. Map the unconditional distribution of Δ logit \Delta_{\mathrm{logit}} , Δ KL \Delta_{\mathrm{KL}} , and A top ​ k A_{\mathrm{top}k} between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} on a fixed corpus, with slice-level concentration. Setup. Identical θ \theta , deterministic sampling, pinned seeds, fixed batch shape; vary one perturbation at a time across precision, attention kernel, and quantisation. Reporting. Per-slice histograms and (p50, p95, p99) of each metric; cumulative top-1 and top-5 disagreement curves. The framework is falsified if the marginal distribution of Δ logit \Delta_{\mathrm{logit}} on any user-facing slice is uncontrolled by any combination of perturbations.

sections.heading: 8.2 E2. Hardware and shape sensitivity
sections.text: How does clause pass-rate degrade as hardware, batch size, and sequence length vary at fixed θ \theta and fixed K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} source build? Report pass-rate heatmaps over (slice × \times regime); cells that narrowly pass or fail are the most important, because they predict where the contract will fail next. Output: slice-scope refinements for Σ \Sigma and routing rules for Π \Pi .

sections.heading: 8.3 E3. RL post-training stability
sections.text: Does the bound of Proposition 2 hold empirically, and what does the importance-correction clause N-RLHF-2 buy at the cost of an extra forward pass per rollout? Run identical PPO and GRPO recipes [ 21 , 23 ] under three rollout configurations: (a) on-policy with K inf = K train K_{\mathrm{inf}}=K_{\mathrm{train}} ; (b) standard inference-engine rollouts with no correction; (c) inference-engine rollouts with the contract-aware correction of Section 6 . Track learning curves, KL-to-reference, win-rates against a held-out reward model, and 𝔼 ⁡ [ w ​ log ⁡ w ] \mathbb{E}[w\log w] . For each failure case (KL collapse, reward hacking, sudden eval drop) identify the clause whose violation preceded it. The bound is falsified if (b) and (c) differ by less than the noise floor on the trajectories the bound predicts will differ most.

sections.heading: 8.4 E4. Contract-aware distillation
sections.text: Can a distillation objective that includes contract penalties produce students with measurably better compliance at neutral or improved task quality? Distil a fixed teacher with ℒ = ℒ task + λ KD ​ ℒ KD + λ 𝒞 ​ ℒ 𝒞 \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}+\lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{C}} , varying λ 𝒞 ∈ { 0 , 0.1 , 1.0 } \lambda_{\mathcal{C}}\in\{0,0.1,1.0\} . Report Pareto frontiers of task quality against clause pass-rate, plus latency, memory, and per-clause sensitivity. The direction claim is falsified if the frontier shifts the wrong way for any λ 𝒞 > 0 \lambda_{\mathcal{C}}>0 .

sections.heading: 8.5 E5. Self-healing routing under fault injection
sections.text: What does contract-aware routing buy over a fixed-kernel baseline under controlled perturbations? Inject synthetic faults (kernel-build regressions, increased quantisation error, hardware degradation) and compare a fixed-kernel deployment against the routing policy of Section 7 . Report MTTR, failed-request fraction, quality preservation during incidents, and false-positive route-switch rate. A policy that recovers faster at a higher false-positive rate is not obviously better; the trade-off is the result.

sections.heading: 8.6 A common reporting template
sections.text: Across all five we report baseline and candidate clause pass-rates per slice, task-quality and reward deltas with confidence intervals, runtime cost deltas, incident metrics (detection lag, rollback success, MTTR), and the contract version evaluated against. A reference implementation following Appendix C can produce all of these artifacts from a single contract file, so reports across experiments and teams remain comparable.

sections.heading: 9 Open questions and research directions
sections.text: The framework is deliberately the smallest object that specifies the gap of Section 1 : four clause families, three violation levels, a four-stage pipeline, and a chain of bounds. Real deployments press on it in four predictable ways, ordered here as a deployed system encounters them: specifying contracts that adapt to context (§ 9.1 ), training models that satisfy them (§ 9.2 ), proving that they hold (§ 9.3 ), and operating gracefully when they do not (§ 9.4 ).

sections.heading: 9.1 Dynamic contracts
sections.text: Static thresholds are easy to audit but brittle. A dynamic contract replaces a fixed τ i \tau_{i} with a context-conditioned envelope τ i ​ ( c ​ ( x ) ) \tau_{i}(c(x)) , where c ⁡ ( x ) c(x) summarises prompt class, sequence length, hardware target, and time of day. One natural instantiation treats threshold selection as a contextual bandit: for each context bucket, learn an envelope that minimises an incident-cost model C ⁡ ( ⋅ ) C(\cdot) subject to a quality-of-service constraint Q ⁡ ( ⋅ ) Q(\cdot) , τ i ⋆ ( c ) = arg ​ max τ − C ( Pr [ violation ∣ τ , c ] ) − λ Q ( τ , c ) , \tau_{i}^{\star}(c)\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{arg\,max}}_{\tau}\;-\,C\!\bigl(\Pr[\text{violation}\mid\tau,c]\bigr)\;-\;\lambda\,Q(\tau,c), (20) with λ \lambda a Lagrange multiplier on quality regression and the search restricted to a vetted hypothesis class so that the resulting envelopes remain auditable. The hardness lives in three places: keeping the controller stable under non-stationary traffic, learning fair envelopes for rare slices that have too little data to support a per-bucket estimate, and governing policy updates that are themselves model artifacts. The third is the most underrated. A dynamic threshold that learns is also a model that ships, and a contract that protects a deployed system from drift cannot be allowed to drift in private.

sections.heading: 9.2 Contract-aware distillation
sections.text: Distillation [ 9 ] aligns a student to a teacher. A contract-aware student additionally satisfies the contract that will govern its deployment: ℒ total = ℒ task + λ KD ​ ℒ KD + ∑ i λ i ​ ϕ i ​ ( m i ​ ( θ s , K inf ) ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KD}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KD}}+\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\,\phi_{i}\!\bigl(m_{i}(\theta_{s},K_{\mathrm{inf}})\bigr), (21) where ϕ i \phi_{i} is a smooth surrogate for the indicator 𝟏 [ m i > τ i ] \mathbf{1}[m_{i}>\tau_{i}] (softplus, hinge). The training objective explicitly accounts for the kernel that will execute the student, which is the level at which the standard distillation literature has consistently underspecified its targets. Three risks shape the research agenda: Goodhart-style overfitting to proxy clauses; the engineering cost of backpropagating through surrogates that depend on the inference kernel; and combining contract terms with preference-based objectives [ 19 ] without destabilising either signal. The first risk is the deepest, because a contract whose clauses can be gamed in training is a contract whose clauses can be gamed at serving time too.

sections.heading: 9.3 Formal verification of clause subsets
sections.text: For a restricted but useful subset of clauses, empirical evidence can be replaced by formal guarantees. Bounded numerical properties such as “for all x x in slice S S and all weights in a region around θ 0 \theta_{0} , Δ logit ​ ( x ) ≤ τ \Delta_{\mathrm{logit}}(x)\leq\tau ” are amenable to interval arithmetic and abstract interpretation in the style of [ 12 , 6 ] . A workable plan has three steps: compile contract clauses to a small DSL with first-order semantics over kernel outputs, as sketched in Appendix A ; translate clauses into properties checkable by interval-bound propagation or SMT, using over-approximations of nonlinearities and quantisation noise; and attach machine-checkable certificates to deployable artifacts, so the serving register holds ( θ , K inf , 𝒞 , proof ) (\theta,K_{\mathrm{inf}},\mathcal{C},\text{proof}) tuples rather than only hashes. The hard problem is scale. Existing verifiers reach only small networks and short sequences, and the gap to deployed transformers is several orders of magnitude on every relevant axis. Compositional and modular verification, in which each block carries a local certificate that composes into a global one, is the only plausible path that does not require a fundamental breakthrough in verifier capacity. Even there, the open questions are real: deriving compositional rules across attention, MLP, and quantisation blocks; treating context-dependent KV-cache states without unrolling the entire history; and propagating certificates through continuous training without re-verifying from scratch after every gradient step.

sections.heading: 9.4 Self-healing kernel routing
sections.text: When contract health degrades, the operational question is not only “roll back?” but also “where do we route now?”. Self-healing routing treats kernel selection as a control problem: given a pool of certified kernels { K 1 , … , K m } \{K_{1},\dots,K_{m}\} with known per-clause profiles, route each request to a kernel that satisfies the most stringent clauses applicable to it, subject to capacity and latency. A natural formulation is a constrained MDP whose state is contract health h t h_{t} and current capacity, whose actions are routing weights over the pool, and whose reward trades quality against contract margin. Existing fleet-management heuristics can then be replaced by policies learned offline from logged incident data and verified to respect hard clauses by construction. The research-level risks are oscillation control under fluctuating health signals, safe exploration when a new kernel is added to the pool with limited prior data, and explainability of routing decisions to safety reviewers whose mental model still treats the fleet as serving a single π θ \pi_{\theta} .

sections.heading: 9.5 How the four directions interlock
sections.text: Dynamic contracts choose the envelope; contract-aware distillation trains models that fit it; formal verification certifies the parts that admit proofs; self-healing routing operates underneath when the envelope is exceeded. Each is incrementally adoptable on top of the static framework.

sections.heading: 10 Related work
sections.text: The framework presented here sits at the intersection of several literatures that have largely run in parallel. RL post-training reasons about policies and gradients but mostly assumes the sampling kernel is the training kernel. High-throughput serving reasons about kernels and hardware but rarely about the gradient consequences of its design choices. Verification reasons about properties but at scales that deployed pipelines exceed by orders of magnitude. Software contracts and SLOs reason about interfaces but were not designed for systems whose outputs are probability distributions over tokens. The kernel contract is a thin specification layer that lets these literatures speak to one another, and the rest of this section positions the paper within each.

sections.heading: RL from human and verifier feedback.
sections.text: The PPO-style pipeline of [ 21 , 17 ] , the trust-region formulation of [ 20 ] , the preference objective of DPO [ 19 ] , and the group-relative variant GRPO [ 23 ] all assume an on-policy or near-on-policy sampling regime. Recent expository work on the engineering practice of RL post-training [ 18 ] catalogues the implementation choices that govern stability but stops short of naming the train–infer kernel pair as a first-class object. Section 6 formalises the bias these methods incur when rollouts come from K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} and gradients from K train K_{\mathrm{train}} , and proposes contract clauses that bound it.

sections.heading: Reproducibility and implementation matters in RL.
sections.text: A line of work documents the fragility of deep RL results to implementation detail: [ 8 ] on benchmark reproducibility, [ 4 ] on the dependence of PPO performance on code-level choices, [ 1 ] on a systematic study of on-policy choices, and [ 11 ] on a reproducible baseline library. The framework here reads these phenomena as a symptom of an unspecified contract between rollout and update kernels; making the contract explicit converts implementation choices from folk knowledge into auditable artifacts.

sections.heading: High-throughput LLM inference.
sections.text: FlashAttention [ 2 ] and its successors [ 3 , 22 ] change accumulation order and tile sizes to maximise hardware utilisation. vLLM [ 13 ] introduces paged KV caches and dynamic batching to maximise throughput. Each is equivalent to a textbook attention or generation algorithm in exact arithmetic but produces non-equivalent outputs in finite precision; they are precisely the sources of ε approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{approx}} and ε sched \varepsilon_{\mathrm{sched}} in Equation 12 .

sections.heading: Quantisation and low-precision compute.
sections.text: FP8 formats are standardised in [ 15 ] . Post-training weight quantisation is studied in GPTQ [ 5 ] and AWQ [ 14 ] . These methods consistently report aggregate quality preservation, but their per-slice and per-task behaviour, which is exactly what contract clauses target, is less systematically reported. The framework gives a vocabulary for that reporting.

sections.heading: Calibration and behavioural drift.
sections.text: [ 7 ] documents the calibration problems of modern networks; label smoothing [ 16 ] is one mitigation. Calibration drift between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} is a natural statistical clause in 𝒮 \mathcal{S} .

sections.heading: Neural network verification.
sections.text: Reluplex [ 12 ] and AI2 [ 6 ] pioneered formal verification of small neural networks via SMT and abstract interpretation. Scaling these methods to modern transformers is open; Section 9.3 proposes the contract DSL as the bridge between operational invariants and what current verifiers can prove.

sections.heading: Hardware lottery and systems-aware ML.
sections.text: [ 10 ] argues that research ideas succeed partly because they happen to match the hardware of their era. Kernel contracts are one way to make the dependence of ML behaviour on the underlying hardware and software stack visible and governable rather than implicit.

sections.heading: Software contracts and SLOs.
sections.text: The contract metaphor is borrowed from design-by-contract programming and the SRE practice of service-level objectives. The contribution of this paper is to instantiate the metaphor for the specific structure of train-infer kernel pairs and to connect it to concrete ML failure modes, including RL gradient bias and quantisation-induced behavioural drift.

sections.heading: 11 Limitations
sections.text: The framework adds machinery, and that machinery has its own failure modes. Six are worth naming explicitly.

sections.heading: Measurement and enforcement overhead.
sections.text: Evaluating clauses, shadowing traffic, and emitting observability artifacts cost compute, storage, and engineering time. The cost is justified at scale and on safety-critical surfaces. It is not justified for small models with non-critical deployments, where simpler regression testing suffices.

sections.heading: Goodhart risk on proxy clauses.
sections.text: Any metric that becomes a target risks being optimised for its own sake [ 7 , 16 ] . Aggressive contract-aware distillation ( Section 9.2 ) may produce students that satisfy proxy clauses while regressing on the underlying behaviour the clauses were meant to protect. Mitigations include holdout clauses that are never used during training, periodic recalibration of τ \tau , and explicit review of clause provenance.

sections.heading: Incomplete observability.
sections.text: On latency-critical paths, emitting full observability artifacts may be infeasible. The contract framework then operates on a sampled subset of traffic, and soft-clause exceedance estimates inherit the bias of that subset. This is tolerable for 𝒮 \mathcal{S} but problematic for 𝒩 \mathcal{N} , where post-incident attribution becomes harder.

sections.heading: Verification scope.
sections.text: The bounds in Section 5 are loose, and formal verification [ 12 , 6 ] currently covers only small slices of the system. We do not claim full proofs of correctness for production-scale transformers; we claim a path along which incrementally more of the system can be brought under formal guarantees.

sections.heading: Recovery logic as a target itself.
sections.text: The routing policy of Section 9.4 is itself a piece of software that can fail. Self-healing systems can oscillate, mis-route, or fail in correlated ways across the fleet. The routing policy should be subject to its own contracts, a meta-contract over Π \Pi , and tested with the same rigour as the kernels it routes between.

sections.heading: Cultural debt.
sections.text: The largest practical risk is not technical. Adopting a contract framework requires research, infrastructure, and product teams to share a vocabulary for what they will and will not tolerate from a deployed model. Without that alignment, the contract becomes a document that no one owns.

sections.heading: 12 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper has developed a framework for specifying acceptable divergence between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} at identical weights θ \theta . A kernel contract 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) packages four clause families that name what divergence is tolerated and where, three violation levels that prescribe a response when bounds fail, a four-stage promotion pipeline that allocates clauses to the venues where they can be checked, and a chain of Lipschitz-style bounds that connects numerical perturbations to behavioural distance and to reward error. None of these pieces is individually novel; the contribution is their composition into an artifact that is versioned and audited together with the model weights and the kernel build. Several consequences follow from making the contract explicit. RL post-training pipelines can bound the bias of the standard policy-gradient estimator with a single clause on the importance ratio ( Section 6 ), and the PPO clipping range ϵ \epsilon acquires a second interpretation as a budget on ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) . Distillation objectives can be written against the kernel that will execute the student. Verification certificates ( Section 9.3 ) can attach to deployable artifacts, so that the serving register holds ( θ , K inf , 𝒞 , proof ) (\theta,K_{\mathrm{inf}},\mathcal{C},\text{proof}) tuples rather than only hashes. Routing policies can respond to contract health rather than only to post-incident signals. Appendix C sketches how each of these artifacts can be produced from a single contract file. The remaining work is empirical. Instantiating the framework on deployed systems, measuring how often pipelines violate their implicit contracts, and quantifying the reliability gain per unit of engineering investment for each of the directions of Section 9 are the natural next steps; Section 8 specifies the protocol against which those measurements would be made.

sections.heading: Appendix A Appendix A: Contract DSL specification
sections.text: This appendix gives a minimal YAML-based contract DSL designed to be consumed by a reference implementation of the form sketched in Appendix C . The DSL is deliberately small. It is meant to be auditable by a reviewer in a single sitting and to compile, for a restricted subset of clauses, into a property checkable by a formal verifier ( Section 9.3 ).

sections.heading: A.1 Schema
sections.text: A contract document has the following top-level structure: ⬇ contract : id : string # stable contract identifier version : string # semver applies_to : model_hashes : [ string ] # weight artifact hashes kernel_hashes : [ string ] # inference kernel build hashes slices : # slice definitions used by clauses - id : string filter : string # boolean expression over request fields clauses : # list of clauses (see below) - id : string family : numerical | statistical | runtime | observability metric : string # name of a registered metric function threshold : number exceedance : number # 0 for hard, >0 for soft level : L1 | L2 | L3 slice_ids : [ string ] remediation : string # one of the actions in escalation_policy escalation_policy : - level : L1 | L2 | L3 action : log | guard | fallback target_kernel : string # optional; required for guard/fallback

sections.heading: A.2 Example: minimal train-infer contract
sections.text: ⬇ contract : id : train_infer_v1 version : 0.1.0 applies_to : model_hashes : [ "sha256:abc..." ] kernel_hashes : [ "vllm-fp8-h100-2026.04" ] slices : - id : all filter : "true" - id : safety filter : "request.category == ’safety’" clauses : - id : N1_logit_drift family : numerical metric : p99_logit_l2 threshold : 0.15 exceedance : 0 level : L2 slice_ids : [ "all" ] remediation : guard - id : S1_topk_agreement family : statistical metric : top5_overlap threshold : 0.98 exceedance : 0 level : L3 slice_ids : [ "safety" ] remediation : fallback - id : R1_p95_latency family : runtime metric : p95_latency_ms threshold : 120 exceedance : 0.01 level : L1 slice_ids : [ "all" ] remediation : log escalation_policy : - level : L1 action : log - level : L2 action : guard target_kernel : vllm - bf16 - h100 - level : L3 action : fallback target_kernel : pytorch - bf16 - reference

sections.heading: A.3 Example: RL post-training stability contract
sections.text: ⬇ contract : id : rlhf_rollout_v1 version : 0.1.0 applies_to : model_hashes : [ "sha256:def..." ] kernel_hashes : [ "vllm-bf16-h100-2026.04" ] clauses : - id : NRLHF1_logw family : numerical metric : mean_abs_log_ratio threshold : 0.05 exceedance : 0.05 level : L2 slice_ids : [ "all" ] remediation : guard - id : NRLHF2_wlogw family : numerical metric : mean_w_log_w threshold : 0.01 exceedance : 0.0 level : L3 slice_ids : [ "all" ] remediation : fallback escalation_policy : - level : L2 action : guard target_kernel : audit - train - kernel - rollout - level : L3 action : fallback target_kernel : audit - train - kernel - rollout Clauses are evaluated independently on their slices. A clause passes on a slice if the measured metric does not exceed its threshold, or, for soft clauses, if the exceedance rate over the evaluation window is within budget. Promotion requires every hard clause to pass on every slice it applies to. Online routing selects the action of the most severe currently-violated clause.

sections.heading: Appendix C Appendix C: Reference implementation
sections.text: This appendix sketches a small Python library, kcc (kernel contract convergence), that maps one-to-one onto the definitions of Section 4 . It is not a production system, nor is it released alongside this paper; the listings below specify the data model, public API, and CLI surface so that a reader can reconstruct the implementation in an afternoon.

sections.heading: C.1 Package structure
sections.text: ⬇ src / kcc / __init__ . py # public API surface contracts . py # Contract, Clause dataclasses; YAML loader metrics . py # registered drift and runtime metrics evaluator . py # ContractEvaluator: runs clauses against kernels policies . py # escalation policies and routing decisions cli . py # command-line entry point: ‘kcc evaluate ...‘

sections.heading: C.2 Core API
sections.text: ⬇ from kcc import Contract , ContractEvaluator contract = Contract . from_yaml ( "examples/contracts/train_infer_v1.yaml" ) evaluator = ContractEvaluator ( train_kernel = train_logits_fn , # callable: x -> logits inference_kernel = infer_logits_fn , runtime_meter = runtime_meter_fn , # callable: x -> {latency_ms, memory_mb} dataset = eval_dataset , slice_definitions = contract . slices , ) report = evaluator . evaluate ( contract ) print ( report . summary ()) report . to_json ( "artifacts/contract_report.json" ) decision = contract . escalation_policy . decide ( report ) print ( decision ) # one of: promote, log, guard:<kernel>, fallback:<kernel>

sections.heading: C.3 Registered metrics
sections.text: The library ships with a small registry of drift metrics: • p{50,95,99}_logit_l2 : percentile bounds on Δ logit \Delta_{\mathrm{logit}} . • mean_kl , p99_kl : distributional drift. • top{1,5,10}_overlap : top- k k agreement A top ​ k A_{\mathrm{top}k} . • mean_abs_log_ratio , mean_w_log_w : importance-ratio diagnostics for RL contracts ( Section 6 ). • ece_gap : calibration drift Δ ECE \Delta_{\mathrm{ECE}} . • p95_latency_ms , p99_latency_ms , peak_memory_mb : runtime metrics. New metrics are registered by decorating a callable with @register_metric(name) ; this makes contract YAML files self-describing.

sections.heading: C.4 Command-line usage
sections.text: The CLI runs a contract against a candidate kernel and emits a structured report: ⬇ kcc evaluate \ -- contract examples / contracts / train_infer_v1 . yaml \ -- train - kernel mypkg . kernels : train_logits \ -- inference - kernel mypkg . kernels : infer_logits \ -- dataset mypkg . datasets : eval_split \ -- output artifacts / report . json The output JSON contains per-clause pass/fail records, per-slice exceedance rates, the computed health score h t h_{t} , and the recommended escalation action.

sections.heading: C.5 Tests
sections.text: An implementation following this sketch is naturally accompanied by unit tests covering metric correctness, exceedance accounting, escalation-policy semantics, and YAML round-tripping; those tests double as executable documentation of the framework’s semantics.

In finite precision the two programs compute measurably different functions of the same weights, with the gap concentrated on slices that aggregate benchmarks under-represent. Off-policy bias in reinforcement-learning rollouts, slice-level regressions under FP8 deployment, calibration drift between fine-tuning and serving, and benchmark scores that fail to reproduce across hardware fleets are facets of this same gap. We formalize the gap as a missing index on π θ \pi_{	heta} and propose a small specification that names it: a kernel contract 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) of numerical, statistical, runtime, and observability clauses with an escalation policy from violations to routing actions. We derive a chain of Lipschitz-style bounds connecting the four families: a single numerical clause on logit drift propagates through total-variation distance into a bound on any bounded reward, with explicit constants. Specialising the chain to RL post-training, we show that a per-token bound on the importance ratio w = π θ K train ​ ( y ∣ x ) / π θ K inf ​ ( y ∣ x ) w=\pi^{K_{\mathrm{train}}}_{	heta}(y\mid x)/\pi^{K_{\mathrm{inf}}}_{	heta}(y\mid x) bounds the bias of the standard policy-gradient estimator under explicit support and norm assumptions, and reinterprets PPO-style ratio clipping as a budget on the train–infer kernel pair rather than only on the policy update. A four-stage promotion pipeline (offline CI, shadow, canary, full) and an online routing loop enforce the contract once a model is deployed. A minimal YAML DSL with a sketched reference implementation ( Appendices A and C ) shows what a deployable artifact of this form looks like. This is a framework and vocabulary paper: we do not report empirical validation at production scale, and we do not claim that kernel divergence is the sole cause of the failure modes the framework addresses. 1 Introduction In a modern post-training pipeline, the symbol π θ \pi_{	heta} denotes two different functions in finite precision. The training path evaluates π θ \pi_{	heta} through a program built around autograd: high-precision accumulators, fixed-shape batches, reference attention, and an operator graph optimised for differentiability. The serving path evaluates it through fused low-precision kernels [ 15 , 5 , 14 ] , a paged key–value cache [ 13 ] , and attention tiles whose sizes depend on the workload [ 2 , 3 , 22 ] . The two programs share parameter tensors and almost nothing else, and the resulting numerical difference is not uniform across inputs: aggregate benchmarks can move within noise while a long-context slice or a safety-critical prompt class moves an order of magnitude more. Reinforcement-learning post-training exposes the same gap. Pipelines such as PPO [ 21 , 17 ] and GRPO [ 23 ] generate rollouts on an inference engine and apply gradients computed on a training engine; the standard estimator’s derivation treats the two as the same policy. The implied per-token importance ratio between rollout time and gradient time is assumed equal to one and is absorbed without flag when it is not, which biases the gradient in a way that does not appear in the training loss and surfaces only later as KL collapse, reward hacking, or sudden reward degradation. The documented fragility of large-scale RLHF to implementation detail [ 8 , 4 , 1 , 11 ] is consistent with this mechanism. The same conflation surfaces wherever the training and inference paths run different programs against the same weights: calibration schedules tuned with K train K_{\mathrm{train}} misfire on probabilities produced by K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} ; benchmark scores diverge across hardware fleets whose unit tests all pass; red-team prompts that fail on one stack pass on the other. We treat them as facets of one specification gap: no pipeline says, in machine-readable form, what divergence between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} it is willing to tolerate, on which slices. This paper develops the object that specifies the gap. A kernel contract is a tuple 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) of numerical, statistical, runtime, and observability clauses with an escalation policy that maps violations to routing actions. The contract sits next to the model checkpoint and the kernel build, is versioned with them, and travels with the artifact through CI and into deployment. Bit-level equivalence is not the target; the inference kernel exists to trade low-level equivalence for throughput, and the trade is worth making. The target is to specify which equivalences are required, where, and what to do when they fail. Section 2 fixes notation and makes the kernel index on π θ \pi_{	heta} explicit. Section 3 collects four failure modes whose shared structure motivates the framework. Section 4 introduces the contract formally. Section 5 derives the Lipschitz-style chain that turns a clause on logit drift into a clause on reward drift. Section 6 specialises the chain to RL post-training. Section 7 describes the four-stage promotion pipeline; Section 8 lays out an experimental protocol against which the framework’s predictions can be tested. Three contributions follow. (i) Conceptual : the right specifiable object in a modern LLM pipeline is the pair ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) together with the slice scope on which they are required to agree, not the checkpoint or the engine alone. (ii) Technical : the chain of Section 5 lets contract authors specify at the level they can measure and inherit guarantees at the level they care about. (iii) Applied : under explicit support and norm assumptions ( Section 6 ), a per-token bound on the importance ratio bounds the policy-gradient bias of the standard estimator, and the PPO clipping range ϵ \epsilon acquires a second interpretation as a budget on the train–infer kernel pair. Scope. This paper proposes a framework and vocabulary. It does not claim that kernel divergence is the sole cause of the failure modes it discusses, does not report empirical validation at production scale, and does not provide a deployable open-source implementation. Section 8 lays out the protocol against which the framework’s predictions can be tested; Appendices A and C specify, in sketch form, what an implementation that consumes its declarative artifacts would look like. 2 Preliminaries The central notational move of this paper is to give π θ \pi_{	heta} the index it has been missing. A kernel K K is the concrete program that, given parameters θ ∈ ℝ d 	heta\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and input x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} , computes logits z θ K ​ ( x ) ∈ ℝ V z^{K}_{	heta}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{V} over a vocabulary of size V V and, when used for optimisation, gradients ∇ θ ℓ 
abla_{	heta}\ell . The induced predictive distribution π θ K ( ⋅ ∣ x ) = softmax ( z θ K ( x ) / T ) \pi^{K}_{	heta}(\cdot\mid x)\;=\;\mathrm{softmax}\! igl(z^{K}_{	heta}(x)/T igr) (1) at temperature T > 0 T>0 depends on K K as well as θ 	heta . Self-healing routing treats kernel selection as a control problem: given a pool of certified kernels { K 1 , … , K m } \{K_{1},\dots,K_{m}\} with known per-clause profiles, route each request to a kernel that satisfies the most stringent clauses applicable to it, subject to capacity and latency. A natural formulation is a constrained MDP whose state is contract health h t h_{t} and current capacity, whose actions are routing weights over the pool, and whose reward trades quality against contract margin. Existing fleet-management heuristics can then be replaced by policies learned offline from logged incident data and verified to respect hard clauses by construction. Each is incrementally adoptable on top of the static framework. 10 Related work The framework presented here sits at the intersection of several literatures that have largely run in parallel. RL post-training reasons about policies and gradients but mostly assumes the sampling kernel is the training kernel. High-throughput serving reasons about kernels and hardware but rarely about the gradient consequences of its design choices. Verification reasons about properties but at scales that deployed pipelines exceed by orders of magnitude. Software contracts and SLOs reason about interfaces but were not designed for systems whose outputs are probability distributions over tokens. The kernel contract is a thin specification layer that lets these literatures speak to one another, and the rest of this section positions the paper within each. RL from human and verifier feedback. The PPO-style pipeline of [ 21 , 17 ] , the trust-region formulation of [ 20 ] , the preference objective of DPO [ 19 ] , and the group-relative variant GRPO [ 23 ] all assume an on-policy or near-on-policy sampling regime. Recent expository work on the engineering practice of RL post-training [ 18 ] catalogues the implementation choices that govern stability but stops short of naming the train–infer kernel pair as a first-class object. Section 6 formalises the bias these methods incur when rollouts come from K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} and gradients from K train K_{\mathrm{train}} , and proposes contract clauses that bound it. Reproducibility and implementation matters in RL. A line of work documents the fragility of deep RL results to implementation detail: [ 8 ] on benchmark reproducibility, [ 4 ] on the dependence of PPO performance on code-level choices, [ 1 ] on a systematic study of on-policy choices, and [ 11 ] on a reproducible baseline library. The framework here reads these phenomena as a symptom of an unspecified contract between rollout and update kernels; making the contract explicit converts implementation choices from folk knowledge into auditable artifacts. High-throughput LLM inference. FlashAttention [ 2 ] and its successors [ 3 , 22 ] change accumulation order and tile sizes to maximise hardware utilisation. vLLM [ 13 ] introduces paged KV caches and dynamic batching to maximise throughput. Each is equivalent to a textbook attention or generation algorithm in exact arithmetic but produces non-equivalent outputs in finite precision; they are precisely the sources of ε approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{approx}} and ε sched \varepsilon_{\mathrm{sched}} in Equation 12 . Quantisation and low-precision compute. FP8 formats are standardised in [ 15 ] . Post-training weight quantisation is studied in GPTQ [ 5 ] and AWQ [ 14 ] . These methods consistently report aggregate quality preservation, but their per-slice and per-task behaviour, which is exactly what contract clauses target, is less systematically reported. The framework gives a vocabulary for that reporting. Calibration and behavioural drift. [ 7 ] documents the calibration problems of modern networks; label smoothing [ 16 ] is one mitigation. Calibration drift between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} is a natural statistical clause in 𝒮 \mathcal{S} . Neural network verification. Reluplex [ 12 ] and AI2 [ 6 ] pioneered formal verification of small neural networks via SMT and abstract interpretation. Scaling these methods to modern transformers is open; Section 9.3 proposes the contract DSL as the bridge between operational invariants and what current verifiers can prove. Hardware lottery and systems-aware ML. [ 10 ] argues that research ideas succeed partly because they happen to match the hardware of their era. Kernel contracts are one way to make the dependence of ML behaviour on the underlying hardware and software stack visible and governable rather than implicit. Software contracts and SLOs. The contract metaphor is borrowed from design-by-contract programming and the SRE practice of service-level objectives. The contribution of this paper is to instantiate the metaphor for the specific structure of train-infer kernel pairs and to connect it to concrete ML failure modes, including RL gradient bias and quantisation-induced behavioural drift. 11 Limitations The framework adds machinery, and that machinery has its own failure modes. Six are worth naming explicitly. Measurement and enforcement overhead. Evaluating clauses, shadowing traffic, and emitting observability artifacts cost compute, storage, and engineering time. The cost is justified at scale and on safety-critical surfaces. It is not justified for small models with non-critical deployments, where simpler regression testing suffices. Goodhart risk on proxy clauses. Any metric that becomes a target risks being optimised for its own sake [ 7 , 16 ] . Aggressive contract-aware distillation ( Section 9.2 ) may produce students that satisfy proxy clauses while regressing on the underlying behaviour the clauses were meant to protect. Mitigations include holdout clauses that are never used during training, periodic recalibration of τ 	au , and explicit review of clause provenance. Incomplete observability. On latency-critical paths, emitting full observability artifacts may be infeasible. The contract framework then operates on a sampled subset of traffic, and soft-clause exceedance estimates inherit the bias of that subset. This is tolerable for 𝒮 \mathcal{S} but problematic for 𝒩 \mathcal{N} , where post-incident attribution becomes harder. Verification scope. The bounds in Section 5 are loose, and formal verification [ 12 , 6 ] currently covers only small slices of the system. We do not claim full proofs of correctness for production-scale transformers; we claim a path along which incrementally more of the system can be brought under formal guarantees. Recovery logic as a target itself. The routing policy of Section 9.4 is itself a piece of software that can fail. Self-healing systems can oscillate, mis-route, or fail in correlated ways across the fleet. The routing policy should be subject to its own contracts, a meta-contract over Π \Pi , and tested with the same rigour as the kernels it routes between. Cultural debt. The largest practical risk is not technical. Adopting a contract framework requires research, infrastructure, and product teams to share a vocabulary for what they will and will not tolerate from a deployed model. Without that alignment, the contract becomes a document that no one owns. 12 Conclusion This paper has developed a framework for specifying acceptable divergence between K train K_{\mathrm{train}} and K inf K_{\mathrm{inf}} at identical weights θ 	heta . A kernel contract 𝒞 = ( 𝒩 , 𝒮 , ℛ , 𝒪 , Π ) \mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{N},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O},\Pi) packages four clause families that name what divergence is tolerated and where, three violation levels that prescribe a response when bounds fail, a four-stage promotion pipeline that allocates clauses to the venues where they can be checked, and a chain of Lipschitz-style bounds that connects numerical perturbations to behavioural distance and to reward error. None of these pieces is individually novel; the contribution is their composition into an artifact that is versioned and audited together with the model weights and the kernel build. Several consequences follow from making the contract explicit. RL post-training pipelines can bound the bias of the standard policy-gradient estimator with a single clause on the importance ratio ( Section 6 ), and the PPO clipping range ϵ \epsilon acquires a second interpretation as a budget on ( K train , K inf ) (K_{\mathrm{train}},K_{\mathrm{inf}}) . Distillation objectives can be written against the kernel that will execute the student. Verification certificates ( Section 9.3 ) can attach to deployable artifacts, so that the serving register holds ( θ , K inf , 𝒞 , proof ) (	heta,K_{\mathrm{inf}},\mathcal{C},	ext{proof}) tuples rather than only hashes. Routing policies can respond to contract health rather than only to post-incident signals. Appendix C sketches how each of these artifacts can be produced from a single contract file. The remaining work is empirical. Instantiating the framework on deployed systems, measuring how often pipelines violate their implicit contracts, and quantifying the reliability gain per unit of engineering investment for each of the directions of Section 9 are the natural next steps; Section 8 specifies the protocol against which those measurements would be made. A clause passes on a slice if the measured metric does not exceed its threshold, or, for soft clauses, if the exceedance rate over the evaluation window is within budget.
